moduleTitle: Pega tools that support Scrum for Business Architects
learningObjectives: Differentiate between Agile Studio and Agile Workbench.
Explain how Agile Studio, the Developer Assistant, and Agile Workbench support and track application development.
Explain how Pulse and Tags enable collaboration.
Explain the role of the product backlog in application development.

elements.description: Pulse provides contextual posts and replies. Developer collaboration is accessible in the studios; a portal navigation Pulse widget must be configured. Default contextual visibility is not made private by an @mention: use Private post and its recipient controls for a restricted conversation.
Tags organize related Cases and Pulse posts. Enter a #tag without spaces; the Tags widget supplies Case-context discovery.
Developer Assistant has Guidance, Knowledge, Work and Checklists tabs. Work opens Agile Workbench; it is not a substitute for acceptance review or project governance.

elements.text: Pulse keeps the conversation with its work context; Tags label related discussions. Visibility and portal placement require deliberate configuration.

bulletPoints: Tags = labels to organize and quickly find work items and discussions.
These tools let Business and IT team members collaborate directly in App Studio.

The Application Profile summarizes the application; its Feature map organizes features/subfeatures and their work items. Blueprint-generated stories are a starting point for refinement, not automatically validated requirements.

elements.description: Agile Workbench is accessible in App Studio and Dev Studio to capture stories, bugs and feedback alongside development. Work items can include screenshots/video and move through To Do, Doing and Done; it is distinct from the standalone Agile Studio application.

A separate, COMPREHENSIVE Pega application for managing Agile/Scrum at scale — organizing backlogs, sprints, teams, releases, user stories, and bugs across projects. Business team members use it to create and organize the artifacts used to manage Scrum.

Use Workbench for contextual capture in either studio. Use Agile Studio for broader project/backlog management. Synchronization requires configured integration; the existence of both tools alone does not establish it.

elements.text: Agile Workbench is the notepad on your desk for jotting issues as you work; Agile Studio is the full project-management command center where the whole program's backlog and sprints are run.

bulletPoints: Workbench is accessible in both studios through its collaboration controls or Developer Assistant Work tab.
Agile Studio = full standalone Agile/Scrum management (backlogs, sprints, teams, releases).
Both, with the Developer Assistant, support and track application development.
Review captured evidence, feature association and status. Imported or Blueprint-generated stories still need collaborative refinement and acceptance criteria.

elements.description: A user story states who needs what and why, with description and testable acceptance criteria. Business and technical participants contribute collectively; the BA is not the only author, the PO approves acceptance criteria, and Developers are responsible for sizing.
Definition of Ready is a locally agreed checklist, not a mandatory universal Scrum artifact. Apply the agreed readiness checks to business and technical stories; typical checks include:

elements.text: Readiness is preparation for planning, not proof of completion. Teams still clarify and adapt work together during a Sprint.

bulletPoints: A ready story has clear acceptance criteria, an estimate/size, priority, and no blockers.
Review stories with business, development, UX and QA participants; use testable outcomes rather than implementation instructions as acceptance criteria.

elements.description: The Product Backlog is the emergent, ordered source of candidate product work. It includes refined items and items needing further elaboration; it is not a fixed promise that all listed work will be built next.

The Product Owner is accountable for backlog ordering with collaborative refinement. Balance near-term readiness and longer-term elaboration. During Sprint Planning, Developers select work with the PO considering the Sprint Goal, capacity and dependencies.

elements.text: An ordered backlog is a changing menu of candidate work. The team plans an achievable Sprint rather than automatically pulling every top item.

bulletPoints: Product backlog = prioritized list of work; the Product Owner maintains/prioritizes it.
Refine near-term work and elaborate longer-term needs; ordering alone does not make every top item ready or guarantee its selection.

examPitfalls.title: Agile Workbench vs. Agile Studio
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Workbench supports contextual capture in App Studio and Dev Studio; Agile Studio is separate project management. Their integration requires configuration.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Quick in-context capture in App Studio → Agile Workbench. Full backlog/sprint/team management → Agile Studio.

examPitfalls.title: Pulse vs. Tags
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Pulse is the in-context conversation feed; Tags are labels for organizing/finding items.

examPitfalls.title: Definition of Ready vs. Definition of Done
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Readiness is about a story being ready to START a sprint (clear, sized, prioritized, no blockers) — not about being finished.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Ready uses a team-agreed checklist for planning. Done requires the Definition of Done and a usable Increment; it does not necessarily require production deployment.

examPitfalls.title: Who owns the backlog
examPitfalls.trapDescription: The Product Owner owns and prioritizes the product backlog; BAs collaborate to refine it.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Backlog ownership/prioritization → Product Owner; BAs help refine stories and acceptance criteria.

examPitfalls.title: Product backlog purpose
examPitfalls.trapDescription: The backlog is the prioritized list that drives Sprint Planning — not a random task pile.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: PO orders the backlog; Developers select Sprint work with the PO considering the Sprint Goal, capacity and dependencies.

examPitfalls.title: Tools support collaboration between Business and IT
examPitfalls.trapDescription: These tools exist so Business and IT collaborate (view/assign/update work) — not just for developers.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Agile Workbench/Agile Studio/Pulse/Tags enable cross-team collaboration and tracking.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A BA wants to capture a bug and a new user story in real time WITHOUT leaving App Studio while building the app. Which tool fits?
practiceQuiz.hint: Agile Workbench is a lightweight, in-App-Studio tool for real-time capture of stories and feedback.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Agile Workbench is the lightweight, in-context tool inside App Studio for capturing/tracking stories, bugs, and feedback in real time. Agile Studio is the separate full Agile-management app.

optionExplanations.A: Workbench captures development items within App Studio.
optionExplanations.B: Standalone Agile Studio is unnecessary for in-context capture.
optionExplanations.C: Predictive decisioning does not track this bug.
optionExplanations.D: Deployment orchestration does not capture user stories.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A program needs to manage backlogs, sprints, teams, and releases across multiple projects in a comprehensive, standalone tool. Which is appropriate?
practiceQuiz.hint: Agile Studio is the full, standalone Agile management application for sprints, backlogs, and teams.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Agile Studio is the comprehensive, standalone Pega application for managing Agile/Scrum at scale (backlogs, sprints, teams, releases). Agile Workbench is lightweight; Pulse/Tags are collaboration features.

optionExplanations.A: Agile Studio supports broader project planning and tracking.
optionExplanations.B: Workbench focuses on contextual work-item capture.
optionExplanations.C: Messages alone do not provide program planning.
optionExplanations.D: Labels alone do not manage releases or capacity.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A new BA joins a Pega project and asks a senior team member when to use Agile Workbench versus Agile Studio during the development process. Which statement best distinguishes the two tools?

options.text: Agile Workbench is accessible in App Studio and Dev Studio; Agile Studio is a separate Agile-management application
Agile Workbench is the standalone enterprise tool; Agile Studio is inside App Studio

practiceQuiz.hint: Workbench is accessible in both studios; Agile Studio is a separate application.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Workbench provides contextual capture in both studios; separate Agile Studio supplies broader management. Configured integration can connect their work items.

optionExplanations.A: Embedded capture and separate project management are complementary.
optionExplanations.B: This reverses where the tools operate.
optionExplanations.C: Integration does not make them identical.
optionExplanations.D: Development tracking is different from deployment orchestration.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Team members want to post messages and replies attached to a specific Case so everyone stays informed. Which feature is this?
practiceQuiz.hint: Pulse is the in-context collaboration feed for team posts, comments, and replies within a Case.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Pulse is the in-context collaboration feed enabling team posts, comments, and replies within a Case. Tags label work items; Decision Tables compute conditional values; Access Roles govern permissions — none of these provide a conversation feed.

optionExplanations.A: Pulse supports discussion in the case context.
optionExplanations.B: Labels group information rather than providing replies.
optionExplanations.C: Conditional decisions do not host conversations.
optionExplanations.D: Permissions do not create a message feed.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A team wants to label related work items so they can be grouped and found quickly later. Which feature should they use?
practiceQuiz.hint: Tags are labels applied to work items and Pulse posts so they can be organized and found later.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Tags label work items and Pulse posts, enabling them to be organized, filtered, and found efficiently. Pulse is the conversation feed; SLAs and Wait Steps are workflow-timing features, not labeling mechanisms.

optionExplanations.A: Tags connect related cases and discussions.
optionExplanations.B: Messages alone do not provide the requested labels.
optionExplanations.C: Deadlines do not label related items.
optionExplanations.D: Pausing work does not organize search results.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Under a team-agreed readiness checklist, which TWO characteristics help make a user story ready for planning?

options.text: It has clear, defined acceptance criteria
It is sized/estimated and prioritized with no blocking dependencies
It has already been deployed to production
It contains the application's Java source code

practiceQuiz.hint: Apply the locally agreed readiness checks, including testable acceptance criteria and sizing.
practiceQuiz.rationale: A and B meet the illustrated readiness checklist. Already deployed is not a prerequisite for starting work, and the Definition of Done does not universally require production deployment. Stories need clear outcomes, not embedded Java source.

optionExplanations.A: Testable acceptance criteria clarify the expected outcome.
optionExplanations.B: Sizing and resolved blockers support a ready story.
optionExplanations.C: Deployment describes completed delivery, not readiness to begin.
optionExplanations.D: Requirements do not need to contain implementation source code.

practiceQuiz.scenario: During a Sprint Planning meeting, a debate arises over who is ultimately responsible for the product backlog. Who primarily owns and prioritizes the product backlog in a Scrum team?
practiceQuiz.hint: The Product Owner owns scope decisions and prioritizes the product backlog for the delivery team.
practiceQuiz.rationale: The Product Owner is accountable for ordering the backlog. BAs, technical leadership, QA and customers contribute expertise and feedback; collaboration does not transfer that accountability.

optionExplanations.A: The Product Owner is accountable for backlog ordering.
optionExplanations.B: Technical leadership contributes but does not own prioritization.
optionExplanations.C: Testing expertise informs rather than owns ordering.
optionExplanations.D: Customers provide input; the PO makes prioritization decisions.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A client stakeholder unfamiliar with Scrum asks a BA to explain the product backlog before a Sprint Planning session. What is the product backlog?

options.text: The prioritized list of user stories/work that drives Sprint Planning

practiceQuiz.hint: The product backlog is the prioritized list of stories and work items that feeds Sprint Planning.
practiceQuiz.rationale: The product backlog is the prioritized list of user stories and work items managed by the Product Owner that feeds Sprint Planning. It is not a Ruleset list, a CI/CD pipeline, or an Insight configuration.

optionExplanations.A: The backlog orders candidate development work.
optionExplanations.C: A pipeline promotes releases, not requirements priorities.
optionExplanations.D: A visualization is not the ordered development workload.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A BA is reviewing user stories with the Product Owner two days before Sprint Planning and finds several stories are incomplete. Why does ensuring user-story readiness matter before a sprint begins?

options.text: It reduces mid-sprint confusion/rework by ensuring stories are clear, sized, prioritized, and unblocked
It guarantees the application never needs testing
It removes the need for a Product Owner
It deploys the story to production automatically

practiceQuiz.hint: Stories reach Definition of Ready so the team can build and test with clarity and confidence.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Readiness gives the team the confidence to build and test, reducing confusion, rework, and mid-Sprint scope changes. It does not remove testing, eliminate the Product Owner's role, or automatically trigger deployment.

optionExplanations.A: Refinement gives the team a shared, buildable requirement.
optionExplanations.B: A clear story still requires testing.
optionExplanations.C: Readiness relies on rather than eliminates PO involvement.
optionExplanations.D: A readiness decision does not run a deployment.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which TWO App Studio collaboration capabilities help Business and IT work together?

options.text: Agile Workbench for capturing/tracking stories, bugs, and feedback
A Wait Step for pausing a Case

practiceQuiz.hint: Pulse handles in-context conversation; Agile Workbench captures and tracks work items in App Studio.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Pulse supports contextual conversation and Workbench captures development work. BIX extracts data and Wait controls Case timing; they do not supply the contextual conversation/capture capabilities requested here.

optionExplanations.A: Contextual messages connect business and technical participants.
optionExplanations.B: Captured stories and feedback make development work actionable.
optionExplanations.C: Data extraction does not manage collaboration items.
optionExplanations.D: A wait controls case timing, not team discussion.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A business stakeholder asks a BA to explain what a user story is during an Agile project kickoff meeting. Which option best describes a user story?

options.text: A concise statement of a business requirement from the user's perspective that the team builds and tests

practiceQuiz.hint: A user story is a concise requirement written from the user's perspective for the team to implement.
practiceQuiz.rationale: A user story is a concise, user-perspective requirement that the team implements and tests. It is not a deployment artifact, an Access Role definition, or a hosting configuration — it is an Agile requirements format.

optionExplanations.A: The story describes a user need and its value.
optionExplanations.B: A deployment package is an implementation artifact.
optionExplanations.D: A hosting plan is infrastructure, not the requirement format.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A BA is preparing a quick reference guide on Pega's collaboration and Scrum tools for new project team members. Which tool-to-purpose pairing is correct?

options.text: Tags → organize and quickly find related work items/posts
Pulse → extract data to external BI tools
Agile Studio → a CI/CD deployment pipeline

practiceQuiz.hint: Match each tool to its actual documented purpose — Tags organize, Pulse converses, Workbench captures work items.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Tags organize and find items. Pulse is for team collaboration (not BIX-style extraction); Agile Studio manages Agile/Scrum (not pipelines); Agile Workbench captures work items (not authentication). Matching each to its correct purpose eliminates the distractors.

optionExplanations.A: Labels help locate related discussions and work.
optionExplanations.B: Pulse supports messages rather than BI extraction.
optionExplanations.C: Agile Studio tracks projects rather than deployment pipelines.
optionExplanations.D: Workbench work items do not authenticate users.

practiceQuiz.scenario: What maintains backlog ordering and helps prepare candidate work for Sprint Planning?

options.text: Ongoing backlog refinement and prioritization by the Product Owner (with BA collaboration)

practiceQuiz.hint: The Product Owner continuously prioritizes and reprioritizes the backlog throughout the project.
practiceQuiz.rationale: PO accountability and collaborative refinement adjust ordering and readiness. Developers select Sprint work with the PO based on the Sprint Goal, capacity and dependencies, not an automatic pull of every top item.

optionExplanations.A: Continual refinement adjusts ordering as business needs change.
optionExplanations.B: Random assignment does not express value priorities.
optionExplanations.C: Ruleset locks do not rank backlog items.
optionExplanations.D: Disabling messaging does not prioritize requirements.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A BA is onboarding new project members and explaining the key differences between Pega's tools that support Scrum ceremonies. Which TWO statements are correct about Pega's Scrum-supporting tools?

options.text: Agile Workbench captures stories/bugs/feedback in real time inside App Studio
Agile Studio manages backlogs, sprints, and teams as a standalone application

practiceQuiz.hint: Workbench is accessible in both studios; Agile Studio is separate project management.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Agile Workbench captures work in App Studio; Agile Studio manages Scrum at scale standalone. Pulse is collaboration (not a pipeline) and Tags organize items (not authentication). No partial credit.

optionExplanations.A: Workbench supports contextual stories, defects and feedback.
optionExplanations.B: Agile Studio adds broader planning and tracking.
optionExplanations.C: Pulse messaging does not deploy applications.
optionExplanations.D: Tags categorize information rather than checking identity.

quickRecap.value: In-context collaboration feed (post/comment/reply) attached to the work.
Labels to organize and quickly find work items and discussions.
Contextual capture in App Studio and Dev Studio; configured integration connects separate Agile Studio.
Separate, comprehensive Pega app to manage Agile/Scrum at scale (backlogs, sprints, teams, releases).
Locally agreed readiness checklist; testable outcomes, collaborative refinement and Developer sizing. Ready is distinct from Done.
Emergent ordered candidate work: PO accountable for ordering; Developers select with the PO considering Sprint Goal, capacity and dependencies.
